strengths: Using label propagation and label spreading within density-ratio Bayesian optimization is a sensible, potentially useful combination. Fixed candidate pools provide a natural setting for exploiting unlabeled input geometry, and the paper also addresses continuous spaces through sampling.

The empirical evaluation covers synthetic functions, tabular hyperparameter optimization, NATS-Bench, and an image-embedding search task. Comparisons against multiple BORE/LFBO classifiers and GP baselines, repeated over 20 seeds with standard errors, provide meaningful evidence of improved sample efficiency on several benchmarks, particularly NATS-Bench.

The paper clearly relates its approach to BORE, LFBO, and established semi-supervised learning methods. The appendices provide useful sensitivity studies covering kernel bandwidth, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, pool subsampling, and threshold ratios, including results where unlabeled data does not help.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the central contribution of unlabeled data. Figure 12 shows that removing transductive learning can improve performance substantially, including on Bukin6 with label propagation and Branin with label spreading. This ablation fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main comparisons learn beta, and the corresponding supervised kernel estimator is absent from the main benchmark comparisons. Matched bandwidth optimization and acquisition selection are needed to distinguish benefits of semi-supervised learning from those of changing the surrogate. The probability-map illustrations also do not establish improved exploration; the random tie-breaking heuristic and simple exploration-augmented BORE/LFBO controls deserve direct evaluation.

The cluster-assumption argument is insufficiently justified. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated inputs does not ensure that high-density connected regions share the objective-threshold label: such regions can cross the unknown decision boundary. Appendix D does not establish that adding unlabeled points reduces the proposed margin or expands the favorable region in a beneficial way. It correctly acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. learning bounds do not directly apply to sequential BO. Consequently, the claimed exploration mechanism remains a hypothesis, and several statements suggesting that the sampling strategy satisfies the assumption should be qualified.

Important implementation choices remain unspecified, limiting reproducibility and assessment of the comparisons. These include input scaling, the label-spreading clamping factor, propagation stopping settings, bandwidth-optimization initialization and bounds, and baseline training and acquisition-optimization details. The use of L-BFGS-B is also not reconciled clearly with selection from arbitrary finite pools such as the MNIST embeddings. A smaller, correctable mathematical inconsistency occurs in Section 4.1: the column-normalized definition of p_ij implies P = W D^{-1} for symmetric W, whereas the text states P = D^{-1} W and subsequently propagates with P transpose.

Evidence for general high-dimensional optimization is limited. The continuous benchmarks are all two-dimensional. The 64-dimensional MNIST experiment uses an embedding trained on 440,000 examples to predict precisely the digit identities defining the optimization objective. Although the separate training and test splits avoid direct test-label leakage, this supplies substantial task-specific supervision and favorable representation structure. Its results therefore provide limited evidence for performance on general high-dimensional black-box objectives.

Computational practicality is not established relative to competitors. Dense graph construction, repeated propagation during bandwidth optimization, and 1,000 acquisition-optimization initializations can introduce substantial overhead. Figure 14 usefully measures sensitivity to pool size, but does not compare runtime against baselines or establish the cost of the adaptive-bandwidth configurations used in the main results. Together with the unresolved attribution and reproducibility issues, this makes weak rejection more appropriate despite the promising benchmark curves.
